text: August fifteenth, 1914. The first ship crosses the Panama Canal.
Eighty-two kilometres, from the Caribbean to the Pacific.
But ships don't sail across Panama. They climb it.
Locks lift them twenty-six metres, up to a lake.
Gatun Lake. A man-made lake of fresh water.
Every ship that crosses uses about two hundred million litres of it.
That's roughly eighty Olympic pools. Per ship.
Then, in October 2023, the canal's watershed had its driest October on record.
Normally, thirty-six ships cross each day. By December, twenty-two.
The canal authority said it was the first time it had ever had to limit crossings.
A shortcut for the world's ships, filled by Panama's rain.
